ety: From va(i)n + -ity, from Middle English vanite, from Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas, from vānus, whence English vain. Doublet of vanitas.

ex: It's not vanity, to me, it's my sanity

ety: From Middle English venquysshen, vaynquisshen, borrowed from a conjugated form of Old French veincre, from Latin vincō.

s.def: To defeat (someone); to overcome.

ety: From Middle English vantage, by apheresis from advantage; see advantage.

ety: From Middle English velvet, velwet, veluet, from Old Occitan veluet, from Vulgar Latin *villutittus, diminutive of villūtus, from Latin villus (“shaggy hair, tuft of hair”). Cognate with French velours.

s.def: A closely woven fabric (originally of silk, now also of cotton or man-made fibres) with a thick short pile on one side.
Very fine fur, including the skin and fur on a deer's antlers.
A female chinchilla; a sow.
The drug dextromethorphan.
Money acquired by gambling.
To cover with velvet or with a covering of a similar texture.
ex: Penmachno mill is situate where a stream has furrowed a deep channel, and velveted the rocks with the richest mosses […].
Last week the scaffolds were up in the hall once more. This time the back wall is to be velveted in absorbent fiber glass […]

s.def: To coat raw meat in starch, then in oil, preparatory to frying.
To remove the velvet from a deer's antlers.
To soften; to mitigate.
ex: She spoke very gently, full of compassion for the boy, velveting her reproach for me.

s.def: to retract.

ety: From the short hairs on the body, which give the crab a velvety texture.

s.def: Necora puber, the largest swimming crab found in British coastal waters.
Any non-violent political revolution, especially the events in Czechoslovakia that led to the velvet divorce.
An arctic sea duck, Melanitta fusca.

ety: From velvet + -een. Compare veloutine, from French.

s.def: A cotton fabric with a short pile, resembling velvet.

ety: From Latin vēna (“vein”) + -al.

s.def: Venous; pertaining to veins.
For sale; available for purchase.
ex: Because lips libertine and and venal had murmured such words to him, he believed but little in the candour of hers; […].

s.def: Of a position, privilege etc.: available for purchase rather than assigned on merit.
Capable of being bought (of a person); willing to take bribes.
Corrupt, mercenary.

ety: From Latin vēna (“vein”) + -ation.

s.def: The arrangement of veins in a leaf, wing, or similar structure.
The hunting of wild animals.

ety: 17th century, likely a backformation from earlier vendible, vendee, vendor inspired by the underlying French vendre, from Old French vendre, from Latin vendere, from vēnum dāre (“to give (something for) sale”).

s.def: Synonym of sell, (now especially) to sell through a vending machine.
To provide or export functionality, especially from an API.
ex: As you've seen, vending FO documents is pretty straightforward from WebObjects. It is just like vending HTML, XHTML, or SVG.

s.def: The act of vending or selling; a sale.
The total sales of coal from a colliery.
The letter Ꝩ/ꝩ, used in Old Norse, related to the rune wynn (ᚹ, whence also Latin-script Ƿ/ƿ) but with the bowl open at the top, like a y.
ex: [...] a gramm. term, implying the use of the old letter 'vend' in spelling v-rungu, v-rangr, v-reiðr, see introduction to letter R; ...

ety: Borrowed from Italian vendetta (“revenge”), from Latin vindicta. See vindicate, avenge.

s.def: A bitter, destructive feud, normally between two families, clans, or factions, in which each injury or slaying is revenged: a blood feud.
ex: The families had been locked in a bitter vendetta for generations.

s.def: Revenge.
A motivational grudge against a person or faction, which may or may not be reciprocated; the state of having it in for someone.
ex: personal vendetta
blood vendetta

ety: This name for such a machine is attested since 1889. The concept of such a machine is centuries older (for more, see Wikipedia at vending machine § History).

s.def: An automatic machine that dispenses merchandise (often food or beverages) in return for payment (originally coins; now also often paper money, credit cards, and wirelessly via digital payment apps).
ex: Meronyms: bill acceptor, card swipe, change slot, coin return, coin slot, flavor strip
It is not clear to all operators of vending machines, though, that their future lies in dispensing meals, rather than snacks or candy.

ety: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman vendor (Old French vendeor), from Latin venditor (“seller”), from vendere (“to sell, cry up for sale, praise”), contraction of venundare, venumdare, also, as originally, two words venum dare (“to sell”), from venum (“sale, price”) + dare (“to give”).

s.def: A person or a company that vends or sells.
A vending machine.
ex: She left her duties guarding the cola vendor and brushed past Earl to the aisle with the creamed corn.

ety: From German Furnier, from furnieren (“to inlay, cover with a veneer”), from French fournir (“to furnish, accomplish”), from Middle French fornir, from Old French fornir, furnir (“to furnish”), from Old Frankish frumjan (“to provide”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną (“to further, promote”). Cognate with Old High German frumjan, frummen (“to accomplish, execute, provide”), Old English fremian (“to promote, perform”). More at furnish.

s.def: A thin decorative covering of fine material (usually wood) applied to coarser wood or other material.
ex: Compartment and corridor partitions are of blockboard, with appropriate decorative veneers to suit the varied interior decoration.

s.def: An attractive appearance that covers or disguises one's true nature or feelings, the veneer of culture.
ex: “Yalda,” Dabashi says, “has managed to survive the centuries because it has been gently recodified with a Muslim veneer.”

s.def: A layer of material placed over a tooth.
To apply veneer to.
ex: to veneer a piece of furniture with mahogany
The stateroom walls are veneered with finely figured English chestnut with the skirting and mouldings in English walnut.

s.def: To disguise with apparent goodness.

ety: From Middle French vénérable, from Old French, from Latin venerabilis.

s.def: Commanding respect because of age, dignity, character or position.
Worthy of reverence.
Ancient, antiquated or archaic.
Made sacred especially by religious or historical association.
Giving an impression of aged goodness and benevolence.

ety: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin venerātus, perfect active participle of veneror (“to worship, venerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To treat with great respect and deference.
To revere or hold in awe.

ety: From Middle French vénération, from Old French veneracion, from Latin veneratio.

s.def: Profound reverence, respect or awe.
The act of venerating or the state of being venerated.
Religious zeal, idolatry or devotion.

ety: From Middle English venereal, venerealle (“of or relating to sexual intercourse”), from Latin venereus, venerius (“of or relating to sexual love”), from Venus (“Roman goddess of love”) (from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”)) + -eus, -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

s.def: Of or relating to the genitals or sexual intercourse.
Of a disease: sexually transmitted; of or relating to, or adapted to the cure of, a venereal disease.
ex: a venereal medicine
[...] I like not his countenance; I am afraid he labours of the venereall murre.
Venereal diseases were responsible for four deaths and 141 final invalidings, [...]

s.def: Pertaining to the astrological influence of the planet Venus; lascivious, lustful.
Of or relating to copper (formerly called Venus by alchemists).

ety: From Middle English venerie, borrowed from Middle French venerie, from Old French venerie (“hunting”), derived from vener, from Latin vēnor (“to hunt”).

s.def: The hunting of wild animals.
Game animals.
The pursuit of sexual indulgence or pleasure.
Cutting open or exposing a vein; a phlebotomy.
ex: His teachings on plethora and venesection remained influential until the nineteenth century.

s.def: Ellipsis of Venetian blind or alternative letter-case form of Venetian.

ety: From Latin Venetianus (“Venetic; Venetian”), from Venetia (“lands of the Veneti; Venice, Veneto; Armorica”) + -anus (“-ian”), from Veneti + -ia. In the case of the Veneti of northern Brittany, derived from Gaulish Uenetoi (“the friendly ones, the kinsmen”), from Proto-Celtic *wenet, a derivation from *wenyā (“kindred”). In the case of the Veneti of northeastern Italy, of uncertain origin but presumably taken from a Venetic endonym, possibly Illyrian or Celtic. Equivalent to Veneto or Venetia +…

s.def: A native or inhabitant of the city of Venice or surrounding province, Veneto region, northeastern Italy.
A native or inhabitant of the surrounding region of Veneto.
A Venetian blind.
Galligaskins.
Synonym of sequin (“type of gold coin”).
The Romance language spoken mostly in the Veneto region of Italy.
The form of this language spoken in Venice.
A blind consisting of overlapping horizontal, flat slats, usually made of metal, vinyl or wood, that can be tilted so as to let in more or less light.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Venezuela, from Italian Veneziola, diminutive of Venezia (“Venice”), after the stilt houses reminiscent of Venetian architecture.

s.def: A country in South America. Official name: Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. Capital and largest city: Caracas.

ety: Etymology tree English Venezuela Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Old French -ainder. Middle English -an English -an English Venezuelan From Venezuela + -an.

s.def: A person from Venezuela or of Venezuelan descent.
ex: The march through the Darién Gap of Haitians, Venezuelans and Cubans fleeing economic collapse and political persecution has been well-documented.

ety: From Anglo-Norman vengeaunce, from Old French vengeance, venjance, from vengier (“to avenge”). Analysable as venge + -ance.

s.def: Revenge taken for an insult, injury, or other wrong.
ex: All the gods have mocked at prayer. This sin must now be punished by the vengeance of men.

s.def: Desire for revenge.
ex: Thereupon full of anger, full of jealousy, full of vengeance, she forms […] a scheme of retribution, […]
If her husband was all forgiveness, asking the bands to play “Dixie,” she was full of vengeance […]

ety: From venge + -ful.

s.def: Vindictive or wanting vengeance.
ex: His chains now broken, the prisoner turned a vengeful eye toward his former captors.
A vengeful mother-of-three has been jailed for 168 days after being convicted of killing a neighbour's kitten by microwaving the 10-week-old pet.

ety: Etymology tree English vengeful Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English vengefulness From vengeful + -ness.

s.def: The state or quality of being vengeful
ex: The vengefulness of the king was legendary.

ety: From Old French venial, borrowed from Late Latin veniālem (“pardonable”), from Latin venia (“forgiveness”).

s.def: Able to be forgiven; worthy of forgiveness.
ex: He did not say that he should favour such an attempt; But he did say that such an attempt would be venial.

s.def: Not causing spiritual death.

ety: From Middle English Venyse, from Old French Venise or Old Italian, from Medieval Latin Venetia, from Latin Venetī + -ia (suffix forming place names), a local tribe in antiquity whose own little-attested language is now known as Venetic. Initial scholarly agreement that they were Illyrian was based on arguments since refuted. They worshipped Belenus and were possibly Celtic or heavily influenced by Celtic culture, despite repeatedly supporting the Romans against the Gauls. Compare the identical…

s.def: A metropolitan city of Veneto, established in 2015; in full, the Metropolitan City of Venice.
A port city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Venice and the region of Veneto, Italy; former capital of an independent republic.
A former province of Veneto.
A former polity in Europe, a republic and colonial empire around the Adriatic and eastern Mediterranean from CE 697 to 1797 with its capital at Venice.
A place in the United States:

ety: From Middle English venisoun, venesoun, from Anglo-Norman veneisun, venesoun, venesun (“meat of large game, particularly deer or boar; hunt”), from Latin vēnātiō, vēnātiōnem (“hunt; meat from a hunt”), formed on vēnātus, perfect participle of vēnor (“to hunt”). Doublet of venatio and venation.

s.def: The meat of a deer, especially one that was hunted in its own natural habitat.
ex: After shooting a deer, field dressing is the next step necessary for high quality venison.

s.def: The meat of an antelope.
ex: 2007, Gregory Simon Bull, Marketing fresh venison in the Eastern Cape Province using a niche marketing strategy (thesis), page xcix

s.def: The meat of any wild animal that has been hunted rather than raised domestically.

ety: Named after British mathematician and philosopher John Venn (1834–1923).

s.def: A diagram representing some sets by contours of closed shapes, such as circles or ellipses (and sometimes also the universal set as a rectangle enclosing all of these shapes), and indicating the relationships between the sets: by overlapping the shapes to show that the corresponding sets have a non…
The intersection of two or more things.

ety: From Middle English venym, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum (“drug; poison; a charm”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”). Doublet of venin and venene.

s.def: An animal toxin intended for defensive or offensive use; a biological poison delivered by bite, sting, etc., to protect an animal or to kill its prey.
ex: […] There may be in the cup / A spider steep’d, and one may drink, depart, / And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge / Is not infected...
I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom.
The serious artist […] [is] obsessed by his material; it’s like a venom working in his blood and the art is the antidote.

s.def: Feeling or speech marked by spite or malice; vitriol.
ex: The venom of such looks, we fairly hope, / Have lost their quality, and that this day / Shall change all griefs and quarrels into love.
History is a study which has none of the venom of reality in it.
The attack was so unwarranted and delivered with such venom that his unpreparedness for it left him speechless.

s.def: To infect with venom; to envenom; to poison.
ex: The Dragon is a venemous beast, and poisoneth all where he lieth; he beats the Earth bare, and venoms it, that it will bear no grass […]

s.def: Poisonous, poisoned; (figuratively) pernicious.
ex: Why should the worm intrude the maiden bud? / Or hateful cuckoos hatch in sparrows’ nests? / Or toads infect fair founts with venom mud?

ety: From Middle English venymous, from Old French venimos, composed of venim (“venom”) + -os (adjective-forming suffix). Synchronically analysable as venom + -ous. Compare Modern French venimeux. Piecewise doublet of venenous.

s.def: Of an animal (specifically a snake) or parts of its body: producing venom (“a toxin intended for defensive or offensive use”) which is usually injected into an enemy or prey by biting or stinging; hence, of a bite or sting: injecting venom.
ex: Do venomous spiders have glands?
[T]he biting of a Pike is venemous and hard to be cured.

s.def: Of or pertaining to venom.
Consisting of, or containing or full of, venom or some other poison; hence, harmful to health due to this.
ex: The villain tricked him into drinking the venomous concoction.

s.def: Posing a threat; dangerous, threatening.
Hateful; malignant; spiteful.
ex: His attitude toward me is utterly venomous.

s.def: Of a weapon such as an arrow or dart: dosed with venom or poison; envenomed, poisoned.
Harmful, hurtful, injurious; specifically, morally or spiritually harmful; evil, noxious, pernicious.
The quality of being venous or venose.
A condition in which the circulation is retarded, and the entire mass of blood is less oxygenated than it normally is.

ety: Morphologically vein + -ous, which is a borrowing from Latin vēnōsus (“full of veins, veiny”), from vēna (“a blood vessel, vein”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of venose.

s.def: Of or pertaining to veins.
ex: Her venous circulation was poor, leading to varicose veins.

s.def: Having passed through the capillaries and given up oxygen for the tissues and become charged with carbon dioxide.
Possessing veins.
ex: It was a sample of venous tissue.

s.def: Having numerous veins.
ex: The tree has highly serrated and venous leaves.

ety: Partly from Middle French vent, from Latin ventus and partly from French éventer. Cognate with French vent and Spanish viento (“wind”) and ventana (“window”). Doublet of wind.

s.def: A slit in the seam of a garment.
To allow gases to escape.
ex: The stove vents to the outside.

s.def: An opening through which gases, especially air, can pass.
ex: the vent of a cask; the vent of a mould

s.def: A small aperture.
An opening in a volcano from which lava or gas flows.
A rant; a long session of expressing verbal frustration.
The excretory opening of lower orders of vertebrates; cloaca.
The opening at the breech of a firearm, through which fire is communicated to the powder of the charge.
In steam boilers, a sectional area of the passage for gases divided by the length of the same passage in feet.
Opportunity of escape or passage from confinement or privacy; outlet.

s.def: Venting (the act by which something is vented)
ex: In some Madras examples which have been successful, the ventage in the under-sluices is about the same as that in the head-sluices above them.

ety: Borrowing from Latin venter (“the belly; the womb; a swelling”).

s.def: A woman with offspring.
A protuberant, usually hollow structure, notably:
A broad, shallow concavity, notably of a bone.
One who vents, who is vocal about feelings or problems.
ex: Venters suffer interpersonally as others avoid their outburst, they become isolated and alone which may result in more venting.

ety: Blend of vent (“wind”) + artifact (“an object shaped or created by some process or agency”) from French vent from Latin ventus

ex: Stones splintered by fire, or faceted by sandstorms (ventifacts or dreikanters) are occasionally mistaken for the work of man.

ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin ventilātus, past participle of ventilō.

s.def: To replace stale or noxious air with fresh.
To circulate air through a building, etc.
To provide with a vent.
To expose something to the circulation of fresh air.
To expose something to public examination or discussion.
To provide manual or mechanical breathing to (a patient).
To breathe.
To shoot with a firearm; to pierce with bullets.
ex: If we went in and there was no burglar, and we got into a shooting with the homeowner and ventilated him, that would be a little difficult to explain.

s.def: To stab (a person).

ety: From ventilate + -or; cf. Latin ventilator.

s.def: A device that circulates fresh air and expels stale or noxious air.
A machine that moves breathable air into and out of the lungs of a patient who is unable to breathe sufficiently.
ex: Near-synonym: respirator

s.def: Some behaviour or happening that relieves a tense atmosphere or situation.
A play or an actor so bad as to empty the theater.

ety: From French ventral, from Latin ventrālis, from venter (“belly, abdomen”); by surface analysis, ventr- + -al.

s.def: Related to the abdomen or stomach.
On the front side of the human body, or the corresponding surface of an animal, usually the lower surface.
On or relating to the sole of the foot or the palmar surface of the hand.
On the lower side of the brain.
Any of the enlarged and transversely elongated scales that extend down the underside of a snake's body from the neck to the anal scale.

ety: From late Middle English, from Latin ventriculus (“the belly”), diminutive of venter (“the belly”). Doublet of ventriculus.

s.def: Any small cavity within a body; a hollow part or organ, especially:
ex: The muscular ventricles pump blood by contracting their fibers in response to electrical stimulation.
“It gave me the wrong one. I thought, wow, if a heart surgeon was using AI to find the lower ventricle… what sort of world would we be living in?”

s.def: distended; corpulent
Broadest in the middle and tapering toward the ends

English -ism English ventriloquism From ventriloquy + -ism.

Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. Middle English -ist English -ist English ventriloquist From ventriloquy + -ist.

ety: Etymology tree Latin venter Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- English ventro- From Latin venter + English -o-.

s.def: Alternative form of ventri-.

ety: Clipping of adventure.

s.def: A risky or daring undertaking or journey.
ex: My heart was beating finely when we two set forth in the cold night upon this dangerous venture.

s.def: An event that is not, or cannot be, foreseen.
ex: A certain man drew a bow at a venture and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness.

s.def: The thing risked; especially, something sent to sea in trade.
ex: My ventures are not in one bottom trusted.

s.def: To undertake a risky or daring journey.
ex: who freights a ship to venture on the seas
A hero ventures forth from the world of common day into a region of supernatural wonder: […]

s.def: To risk or offer.
ex: to venture funds
to venture a guess
Nothing ventured, nothing gained.

s.def: To dare to engage in; to attempt without any certainty of success.
To confide in; to rely on; to trust.
ex: A man would be well enough pleased to buy silks of one whom he would not venture to feel his pulse.

s.def: To say something; to offer an opinion.
To put or send on a venture or chance.
ex: to venture a horse to the West Indies

ety: From venture + -some.

s.def: Adventurous; bold; willing to take risks.
Potentially hazardous; risky.

ety: Etymology tree English venture Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English venturous From venture + -ous.

s.def: Adventurous; venturesome; willing to undertake activities involving risk.

ety: From Middle English venu, from Old French venue, the feminine singular past participle of the verb venir (to come). Doublet of veny.

s.def: A theater, auditorium, arena, or other area designated for sporting or entertainment events.
A neighborhood or near place; the place or county in which anything is alleged to have happened; also, the place where an action is laid, or the district from which a jury comes.
ex: The twelve men who are to try the cause must be of the same venue where the demand is made.

s.def: A bout; a hit; a turn.
A stadium or similar building in which a sporting competition is held.
The place where something happens; especially, one formally recognized as an appropriate one for that occurrence.
ex: Near-synonym: setting
The metalworking forum is not the venue for this discussion about politics.
A care transition often involves a change in venue, which presents a risk of missed follow-up.

s.def: A group of vultures.
ex: In as little as twenty minutes, a venue of vultures can rip apart and dispose of an eight-hundred-pound cow carcass.
the goat was entirely concealed by a venue of vultures turned inwards , wings flaring , heads moving up and down , feathers flashing in the sunlight
As Angelina pulled in and got out of her car, she looked through her binoculars and there appeared to be small venues of vultures everywhere

ety: From translingual Venus (“a genus of clams”), from Latin.

s.def: Any of the bivalve molluscs in the genus Venus or family Veneridae.

ety: Etymology tree Latin Venusbor. Middle English Venus English Venus Inherited from Middle English Venus, borrowed from Latin Venus.

s.def: The second planet in the Solar system.
ex: Near-synonyms: morning star, Phosphorus, Eosphorus, Lucifer; evening star, Vesper, Hesperus
Venus rises on the 1st day 1/4 to 5 a.m., and 4h. 25m. a.m. on the last day. […] She is now beginning to move northward.

s.def: The goddess of love, beauty, fertility, and sexuality, or a depiction thereof.
ex: Of all the classic Venuses known to us in modern times, this Venus of Milo is certainly the most popular.

s.def: A female given name.

ety: From Venus (after the resemblance of the leaves to a human vulva) + flytrap (after the insectivorous nature of the plant).

s.def: An insectivorous plant (Dionaea muscipula) of the savannas of North and South Carolina, with hinged leaves bordered with stiff hairs that close when an insect alights on them.
A kind of barbed trap used in the Vietnam War.

ety: Ultimately from Veps veps.

s.def: The Veps language, spoken by the Vepses, belonging to the Finnic group of the Finno-Ugric languages.

ety: From Latin vērāx (“truthful”) + -acious, from vērus (“true”).

s.def: True.
ex: The politician's statement was eventually proven to be veracious.

s.def: Truthful; speaking the truth.
ex: Now there are two curious circumstances to be observed in this relation of my uncle's, who was, as I have said, a perfectly veracious man.

ety: From Middle French véracité, from Old French veracitie, from Medieval Latin vērācitās (“truthfulness”) (whence -acity), from Latin vērāx (“truthful, speaking truth”), from vērus (“true, real”). See very.

s.def: The quality of speaking or stating the truth; truthfulness.
ex: Of course if you don't accept Conway's story, it means that you doubt either his veracity or his sanity—one may as well be frank.

s.def: Something that is true; a truthful statement; a truth.
Agreement with the facts; accordance with the truth; accuracy or precision.
Act of being exact and accurate.
Correctness and carefulness in one's plan of action.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Veracruz.

s.def: city in Mexico
A coastal state in southeastern Mexico.
A city in Veracruz, Mexico.
A surname from Spanish.

ety: An Indian English word of Indo-Portuguese origin, from Portuguese varanda (“balustrade; balcony”). Further etymology is unclear and disputed.

s.def: A gallery, platform, or balcony, usually roofed and often partly enclosed, extending along the outside of a building.
ex: Boulte ate his breakfast, advised her to see her Arab pony fed in the veranda, and went out.
Our part of the veranda did not hang over the gorge, but edged the meadow where half a dozen large and sleek horses had stopped grazing to join us.

ety: From Middle English verbe, directly from Latin verbum (“word, verb”), reinforced by Old French verbe, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo-. Doublet of verve and word.

s.def: A word that indicates an action, event, or state of being.
ex: The word “speak” is an English verb.

s.def: Any word; a vocable.
ex: a Verb of the Singular

s.def: An action as opposed to a trait or thing.
ex: Kindness is a verb, not an adjective. You're only kind if you do kind things.

s.def: A named command that performs a specific operation on an object.
A phrase that functions syntactically as a verb, consisting of a main verb and any auxiliaries.
A construction in a clause consisting of a verb and its internal complements, or modifiers.

ety: From Old French verbal, from Late Latin verbālis (“belonging to a word”). Equivalent to verb + -al.

s.def: Expressly spoken rather than written; oral.
ex: a verbal contract
a verbal testimony
You can't have verbal communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.

s.def: A verb form which does not function as a predicate, or a word derived from a verb. In English, infinitives, participles and gerunds are verbals.
Of or relating to words.
Concerned with the words, rather than the substance of a text.
Consisting of words only.
ex: We subjoin an engraving […] which will give the reader a far better notion of the structure than any verbal description could convey to the mind.
It was not a verbal remark, but a proceeding in dumb-show

s.def: Derived from, or having the nature of a verb.
Used to form a verb.
Capable of speech.

s.def: Abounding with words; verbose.

ety: Partly from Middle French verbaliser and partly from verbal + -ize.

ety: Attested in English since 1481 (therefore considered a Middle English derivation by some): from Medieval Latin verbātim (“word for word”), from Latin verbum (“word”) + -ātim (adverbial suffix).

ex: I have copied his speech verbatim, so this is exactly what he said, word for word.

ex: Ironically, verbatim note taking can interfere with listening attentively.

ety: Borrowed from Latin verbēna (“leaves or twigs of olive, myrtle, laurel, or other sacred plants employed in religious ceremonies”), from Proto-Indo-European *werbʰ-. Doublet of vervain, via French.

ex: Linda pulled a piece of verbena and crumpled it, and held her hands to her mother. -
Hidden behind a large stone urn full of verbena, Dottie watched as her enemy greeted Johnny at the door.

ety: From French verbiage. Compare verb meaning "word" in verbal and verbose.

s.def: Overabundance of words.

Use concise military verbiage.

To talk; to chat.

ety: From Latin verbōsus (“prolix, wordy, verbose”). Verbōsus is derived from verbum (“word”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to say, speak”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, overly, prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Equivalent to verb + -ose.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from German verboten (“banned, forbidden, prohibited”). Doublet of forbidden.

ety: From Middle French verdoyant, from Old French verb verdier, verdoier, from vert (“green”), from Vulgar Latin *virdis, from Latin viridis.

Inexperienced.

ety: From Middle English verdit, from Anglo-Norman verdit (> Medieval Latin veredictum), from veir (“true”) + dit (“saying”); possibly a calque of a Germanic term such as Old English sōþword, sōþsprǣċ, sōþspell, sōþsagu, or sōþcwide, all meaning "true story, statement of truth, account, history". We've reached a verdict on your proposal.

ety: From Middle English vertegrece, verdegres, from Old French verte grez (literally “acidic green”), an alteration of older verte de Grece (literally “green of Greece”). The modern French writing of this word is vert-de-gris (literally “green of gray”).

ex: Let's to^([sic]) the museum. Cannon-balls; arrow-heads; Roman glass and a forceps green with verdigris.

ety: Inherited from Middle English verdure, from Middle French verdure, from Old French verdure, from Late Latin *viridūra, from viridis (“green”) + -ūra (abstract noun-forming suffix).

ety: Borrowed from Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”), hence "scope, territory dominated", from Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”), of unknown origin. The spindle of a watch balance, especially one with pallets, as in the old vertical escapement.
To be or come very close; to border; to approach.

s.def: To bend or incline; to tend downward; to slope.

A lay person who takes care of the interior of a church and acts as an attendant during services, where he or she carries the verge (or virge). In the United States, the office is generally combined with that of sexton.
ex: As soon as we were all in the night the verger rolled shut the doors and blotted out the chandeliers.

ety: From Latin veridicus (“truly said”), from verus (“true”) and dīcō (“to say”).

Pertaining to an experience, perception, or interpretation that accurately represents reality.
ex: Few believe that all claimed religious experiences are veridical.
There was great need for empirical research that would build a more veridical description of organizations and management.

ety: From Middle French verification (modern French vérification) or its etymon Medieval Latin vērificātiō. By surface analysis, verificate + -ion.

ety: From Old French verifier (French: vérifier), from Medieval Latin vērificāre (“make true”), from Latin vērus (“true”) + faciō (“do, make”); see -fy.

ety: From Middle French vérisimilitude, from Latin vērīsimilitūdō (“likeness to truth”), more correctly written separately as vērī similitūdō; from vērī, genitive singular of vērus (“true, real”), + similitūdō (“likeness, resemblance”).

Connected to a collective memory; not imported.

The moment at which the Sun crosses the celestial equator, appearing to tilt toward the observer, occurring in March in the Northern Hemisphere and in September in the Southern Hemisphere.

ety: From New Latin vernātiō, from Latin vernāre (“to be verdant, to flourish”) + -tiō (“-tion”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from vernus (“springlike”) + -āre (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥. Equivalent to vernal + -tion.

The arrangement of multiple organs (such as leaves and flower parts) within a bud.

To draw a muleta over and away from a bull's face in bullfighting.

The overall slope of a region.

Having varied uses or many functions.
Changeable or inconstant.
Capable of moving freely in all directions.

Capable of being either a dominant or a submissive partner in a sexual relationship.

He clenched his fists in vexation and looked up at her impetuously.
He gave the doctor a look of vexation. He was surprised to see him, and resented the intrusion.

s.def: A source of mental distress or trouble; an affliction, a woe; also, a source of annoyance or irritation; an annoyance, an irritant.
ex: She did harass Helen to give me up; but, after all, poor woman, I believe I have been a great vexation to her, and I cannot help being sorry for her.

ety: From Middle English vyaund, from Anglo-Norman and Old French viande, from Late Latin *vivanda, from Latin vīvenda, from the verb vīvō (“to live”). Compare victual, viando. ety: The adjective (then also used as a participle) is first attested in 1420, in Middle English, the verb in 1620; partly from Middle English vibrat(e) (“reverberant”), partly directly borrowed from Latin vibrātus, perfect passive participle of vibrō (“to agitate, set in tremulous motion”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyp- (“to oscillate, swing”) or *weyb-.

A loyal supporter or devoted admirer of a person or institution.
ex: Well then, ye who delight in laughter, ye who are votaries of the proverb, "Laugh and grow Fat;"

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁wegʷʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Indo-European *h₁wogʷʰéyeti Proto-Italic *woɣʷeō Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Italic *-tos Proto-Italic *woɣʷetos Proto-Italic *wowitos Latin vōtus Latin vōtumder. English vote From Latin vōtum, a form of voveō (“to vow”) (cognate with Ancient Greek εὔχομαι (eúkhomai, “to vow”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wegʷʰ- (“to promise, to vow”). Doublet of vow.

s.def: formalised choice
A formalized choice on legally relevant measures such as employment or appointment to office or a proceeding about a legal dispute.
ex: The city council decided the matter should go to public vote.
Parliament will hold a vote of confidence regarding the minister.
One occasion indicative votes were used was in 2003 when MPs were presented with seven different options on how to reform the House of Lords.

s.def: An act or instance of participating in such a choice, e.g., by submitting a ballot.
ex: The Supreme Court upheld the principle of one person, one vote.
If you vote once, you're considered a good citizen. If you vote twice, you face four years in jail.

s.def: An ardent wish or desire; a vow; a prayer.
A formalized petition or request.
Any judgment of intellect leading to a formal opinion, a point of view.
Any judgment of intellect leading not only to a formal opinion but also to a particular choice in a legally relevant measure, a point of view as published.
ex: dissenting vote (i.e. in particular the differing opinion published with a judicial judgment considered as a source of information)

s.def: To cast a vote; to assert a formalized choice in an election.
ex: Q: Did you vote last month? A: Yes. I voted for John Smith, and it's a shame that he lost; you can't blame me for the mess we're in now.
The directors voted on the question of whether to increase the R&D spending.
To vote on large principles, to vote bravely, requires a great amount of information.

s.def: To choose or grant (some objective) by means of a vote, or by general consent.
ex: The directors voted an increase in R&D spending.
The meal was voted a great success.

s.def: To exercise one's voting right upon (a ballot or a share of stock).
ex: vote your ballot
vote your shares
Please vote your ballot using black or blue ink, then seal your ballot inside the privacy envelope.

ety: From vote + -er.

s.def: Someone who votes or is entitled to vote.
ex: The exact question being put to voters for a yes or no answer is: “Should Iceland reopen accession negotiations with the European Union?”

ety: From Vote + -ic, named after the Votes who speak it.

s.def: A nearly extinct Finno-Ugric language spoken in Ingria.
A small enclosed compartment where a voter may register a vote in private; it may house some voting machine, or just have a pencil for marking a voting slip.

a piece of paper with a list of the candidates at an election (sometimes with an indication of the candidate's party); the voter puts an X in the corresponding place against the candidate of his choice, folds the slip and places it in a ballot box provided.

ety: The verb is derived from Middle English vouchen (“to call, summon; to provide; to make available, proffer; to affirm, declare formally”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman vocher, voucher, woucher, and Old French vocher, voucher, vochier (“to call, summon; to claim; to call upon, invoke; to denounce”) [and other forms], from Vulgar Latin *vocicāre, derived from Latin vocāre (“to call, summon; to call upon, invoke; to designate, name; to bring or put (into a condition or state”), ultimately fr…

s.def: To call on (someone) to be a witness to something.
To cite or rely on (an authority, a written work, etc.) in support of one's actions or opinions.
To affirm or warrant the correctness or truth of (something); also, to affirm or warrant (the truth of an assertion or statement).
To bear witness or testify to the nature or qualities (of someone or something).
To back, confirm, or support (someone or something) with credible evidence or proof.
Synonym of vouchsafe (“to condescendingly or graciously give or grant (something)”).
To assert, aver, or declare (something).
ex: [W]hat we have done None shall dare vouch, tho' it be truly known; […]

s.def: In full vouch to warrant or vouch to warranty: to summon (someone) into court to establish a warranty of title to land.
Followed by over: of a vouchee (a person summoned to court to establish a warranty of title): to summon (someone) to court in their place.
To guarantee legal title (to something).

ety: From vouch + -er. The verb is from the noun.

s.def: A piece of paper or other token that entitles the holder to a discount, or that can be exchanged for goods and services.
ex: a voucher for a free kettle
This voucher entitles the bearer to a 20% discount on frozen goods.

s.def: A receipt.
One who or that which vouches.
ex: To the fashionable world he cannot be a stranger […] and his having married a sister of the Duke of Leeds is a voucher for my assertion.

s.def: A copy of a published advertisement sent by the agency to the client as proof of publication.
A mechanical device used in shops for automatically registering the amount of money drawn.
To establish the authenticity of; to vouch for.
To provide a vouch for (an expenditure).
To provide (a beneficiary) with a voucher.

ety: From vouch + safe, written as two words in Middle English and early Modern English.

s.def: To graciously give, to condescendingly grant a right, benefit, outcome, etc.; to deign to acknowledge.
ex: Needless to say, we have been vouchsafed no idea of what this might cost the innocent victims, the ratepayers.

s.def: To receive or accept in condescension.
To disclose or divulge.
ex: She vouchsafed to me that she regretted ever marrying him.
What have the gods told you? What have you foreseen? The gods have vouchsafed me nothing, told me nothing.
His predictions were at first to be guided by direct intimations vouchsafed to him by the god; […]

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French voussoir, from Old French vosoir, from Vulgar Latin *volsorium, from *volsus, from Latin volvō (“to roll”).

s.def: One of a series of wedge-shaped bricks or stones forming an arch or vault.
ex: Other areas have mortar joints missing, including between the voussoir blocks forming the edge of the arches on either side of the pier.

ety: Inherited from Middle English vowe, voue, that from Old French vut, in turn from Latin vōtum (“a promise, dedication, vow”), from vovēre (“to promise, vow”). Not related to avow. Doublet of vote.

s.def: A solemn promise to perform some act, or behave in a specified manner, especially a promise to live and act in accordance with the rules of a religious order.
ex: The old hermit, up in the mountains, took a vow of silence.

s.def: A declaration or assertion.
A votive offering.
To make a vow; to promise.
ex: We do not vow that we will never sin, nor neglect a duty (nor ought we to do so).

s.def: To make a vow regarding (something).
ex: The wronged woman vowed revenge.

s.def: To declare publicly that one has made a vow, usually to show one's determination or to announce an act of retaliation.
ex: The rebels vowed to continue their fight.

ety: From Middle English vowel, from Old French vouel, a variant of voyeul (whence French voyelle), from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”), itself a semantic loan of Koine Greek φωνῆεν (phōnêen). Doublet of vocal and vocalis.

s.def: A sound produced by the vocal cords with relatively little restriction of the oral cavity, forming the prominent sound of a syllable.
ex: Hawaiian has either five or twenty-five vowels, depending on how they are counted.

s.def: A letter or diacritic representing the sound of a vowel; in English, the vowels are a, e, i, o, u, y (sometimes), and w (rarely).
ex: The word facetiously is spelled with all six vowels in alphabetical order.
The word cwm, borrowed from Welsh, is an example of the letter w serving as a vowel in English.

s.def: To add vowel points to a consonantal script (e.g. niqqud in Hebrew or harakat in Arabic).

A phonological process in some languages that sets constraints on which vowels may be found near each other or within a word, such as back vowels or front vowels; sometimes resulting in variant affixes, clitics or similar variations.
ex: Vowel harmony is an important aspect of Mongolian.

ety: From vowel + -ize.

s.def: To give the quality, sound, or office of a vowel to.
To insert a vowel or vowels into.
ex: One approach is to have experts in Arabic manually vowelize a small training set.

ety: Blend of volumetric + pixel.

s.def: The three-dimensional analogue of a pixel; a volume element representing some numerical quantity, such as the color, of a point in three-dimensional space, used in the visualization and analysis of three-dimensional (especially scientific and medical) data.

ety: From Middle English viage, borrowed from Anglo-Norman viage and Old French voiage, from Latin viaticum. The modern spelling is under the influence of Modern French voyage. Doublet of viaticum.

s.def: A long journey, especially by ship.
ex: He went on a voyage to France.

s.def: A written account of a journey or travel.
The act or practice of travelling.
ex: [...] [A]ll Nations haue Enterknowledge one of another, either by Voyage into Forreine Parts, or by Strangers that come to them: [...]

s.def: To go on a long journey.
ex: A mind forever voyaging through strange seas of thought alone.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Canadian French voyageur.

s.def: A trader, particularly in furs, who worked (and explored) in the area of Canada and the northern United States from the 16th to early 19th centuries; they were often of Quebecois extraction.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *widéh₁yeti Proto-Italic *widēō Latin videō Old French veoir Middle French veoir French voir Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French voyeurbor. English voyeur Borrowed from French voyeur, from voir (“to see”).

s.def: A person who derives sexual pleasure from observing other people engaging in some intimate or sexual activity; one who engages in voyeurism.
An obsessive observer of sensational or sordid subjects.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *widéh₁yeti Proto-Italic *widēō Latin videō Old French veoir Middle French veoir French voir Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French voyeurbor. English voyeur Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Gre…

s.def: The derivation of sexual satisfaction by watching unsuspecting people secretly, especially when those being watched are undressed or undressing, toileting, or engaging in sexual activity.
The derivation of satisfaction by obsessively watching or following sensational or sordid subjects.

ety: Borrowed from German Völkerwanderung.

s.def: Migration Period

ety: Borrowed from French vraisemblance.

s.def: verisimilitude
ex: Recognition of this first level of vraisemblance need not depend on the claim that reality is a convention produced by language.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Vuelta a España (literally “Tour of Spain”).

s.def: An annual long-distance cycling race in Spain.

ety: From Vulcan (“inhabitant of the fictional planet Vulcan in the television series Star Trek”) + salute. The gesture was devised by the American actor Leonard Nimoy (1931–2015), who portrayed the half-Vulcan character Spock in the television series Star Trek (originally broadcast 1966–1969); he first used it in “Amok Time”, the first episode of the second season aired on September 15, 1967.

s.def: A gesture of greeting among Star Trek fans, consisting of a raised hand with the palm forward and the thumb extended, and the fingers parted between the middle finger and ring finger.
ex: They may exchange Vulcan salutes in greeting as a sign of in-group status—the in-group being Star Trek fans rather than Vulcans.

s.def: A hardened rubber made by vulcanization of latex with sulfur.
A rare mineral, copper telluride.

ety: Etymology tree English Vulcan Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English vulcanize From Vulcan + -ize.

s.def: To treat rubber with heat and (usually) sulfur to harden it and make it more durable.
To undergo such treatment.
ex: These vulcanized hearts, they only become more resistant when you ask for mercy.
Natural rubber […] vulcanizes readily at the double bonds to give a strong cross-linked structure.

ety: From Middle English vulgare, from Latin vulgāris, from volgus, vulgus (“mob; common folk”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Compare Welsh gwala (“plenty, sufficiency”), Ancient Greek ἁλία (halía, “assembly”), εἰλέω (eiléō, “to compress”), Proto-Slavic *valъ.

s.def: Debased; uncouth; distasteful; obscene.
ex: vulgar language
vulgar words
a truly vulgar showing of affection

s.def: Having to do with ordinary, common people.
ex: Near-synonyms: vulgate; vulgarized
It might be more useful to the English reader […] to write in our vulgar language.
The mechanical process of multiplying books had brought the New Testament in the vulgar tongue within the reach of every class.

s.def: Common, usual; of the typical kind.
ex: vulgar bush brown (Bicyclus vulgaris)

s.def: Being a vulgar fraction.
ex: A fraction is vulgar if it has one integer divided by another integer, as long as the integer that's doing the dividing isn't equal to zero.

s.def: A common, ordinary person.
The common people.
The language of a people, especially the commoners.

ety: From vulgar + -ian. Compare Late Latin vulgārius, Latin vulgāris.

s.def: A vulgar individual, especially one who emphasizes or is oblivious to his or her vulgar qualities.
ex: She is a bitch in heat, a mindless grinning vulgarian, and a shrewd and desperate schemer all at once.

ety: Etymology tree English vulgar Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English vulgarism From vulgar + -ism.

s.def: Vulgarity.
A word or term that is considered offensive or vulgar.
ex: "Shit" is a vulgarism.

s.def: A spelling, word, or phrase used in common speech that is considered improper or incorrect for formal communication.
ex: Editors of newspapers allow more vulgarisms to go to print today than they used to.

ety: Etymology tree English vulgar Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English vulgarize From vulgar + -ize.

s.def: To make vulgar.
ex: Words only vulgarize love and blunt its edge.

ety: From Latin vulgātus, past participle of vulgō (“publish, make common, cheapen”).

s.def: Made common, published for common use.
In or pertaining to the common version or edition.
The language of a people, especially the commoners.
ex: English sentences were often described in ways more appropriate to Latin than to the spoken vulgate (Lindemann 78-79).

s.def: A common version or edition.
To publish, spread, promulgate to the people.
ex: Ordinary and vulgated sources will usually give all that is needed for a broad outline
we have seen this in the way in which the affair of Capri has been everywhere vulgated, amid endless perversion and distortion
Amongst the traditional vulgated anecdotes floating about the world

ety: From vulnerable + -ity.

s.def: The state of being vulnerable; susceptibility to attack or injury, either physical or emotional; the state or condition of being weak or poorly defended.
ex: Near-synonym: weakness
The country recognized their defence vulnerability after an airplane landed in front of the central square without any consequences.
The only disadvantage of timber snow fencing is its extreme vulnerability to fire.

s.def: computing: type of weakness
A specific weakness in the protections or defences that (literally or figuratively) surround someone or something.
ex: Near-synonyms: flaw, weakness, liability

ety: From Late Latin vulnerābilis (“injurious, wounding”), from Latin vulnerō (“to wound”).

s.def: More or most likely to be exposed to the chance of being attacked or harmed, either physically or emotionally.
ex: You are vulnerable to be bullied by someone at school.

s.def: More likely to be exposed to malicious programs or viruses.
ex: a vulnerable PC with no antivirus software

s.def: at moderate risk of extinction though not quite endangered.
ex: Welsh is merely a vulnerable language, but Irish and Scottish Gaelic are definitely endangered.

ety: From Latin vulnerārius, from vulnus (“wound”).

s.def: Useful or used for healing wounds; curative, healing.
ex: Take, for example, the famous vulnerary ointment attributed to Paracelsus.

s.def: Causing wounds; wounding.
A healing drug or other agent used in healing and treating wounds.

ety: Named by the astronomer Johannes Hevelius in 1687. From Latin vulpēcula (“little fox”).

s.def: A faint autumn constellation in the northern sky.

ety: Borrowed from Latin vulpīnus (“foxy, fox-like”), from vulpēs, earlier volpēs (“fox”), from Proto-Indo-European *wl(o)p- (“fox”). Cognate with Welsh llywarn (“fox”), Ancient Greek ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx), Armenian աղուէս (aġuēs), Albanian dhelpër, Lithuanian vilpišỹs (“wildcat”), Sanskrit लोपाश (lopāśa, “jackal, fox”).

s.def: Pertaining to a fox.
Having the characteristics of a fox; foxlike; cunning.
Any of certain canids called foxes (including true foxes, arctic foxes and grey foxes), distinguished from canines, which are regarded as similar to dogs and wolves.
A person considered cunning.

ety: Borrowed into Middle English from Anglo-Norman vultur, from Old French voutoir, voutre, from Latin vultur, voltur. Displaced native Old English ūf.

s.def: Any of several carrion-eating birds of the families Accipitridae and Cathartidae.
ex: In clusters on the plain, like cowlless monks at matins, sat the vultures that had settled on the corpse of the hyena impaled by the female rhino […]

s.def: A person who profits from the suffering of others.
ex: Within ten minutes of the accident, the vultures appeared and were organizing lawsuits.

s.def: To circle around one's target as if one were a vulture.
ex: Rudy vultured when asking the girl out.

s.def: ravenous; rapacious

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, earlier volva (“womb, female sexual organ”), probably from volvō (“to turn, wrap around”). Akin to Sanskrit उल्ब॑ (úlba) and उल्व॑ (úlva, “womb”) or English valve, valva and other descendants of the Latin term (evolve, involve, revolve).

s.def: The external female genitalia of humans and other placental mammals, which includes the clitoris, labia, and vulval vestibule/vulvar opening.
ex: The vulvae of the sow were popular as a gourmet's dish. Credited with erotic effects.
The wedge-shaped character was the triangle, the archaic Paleolithic sign of the vulva; the pubic triangle was at the end of the phallic stylus.

s.def: A protrusion on the side of a nematode.

ety: From vulvo- + -odynia.

s.def: Pain in the vulva unexplained by vulvar or vaginal infection or skin disease.
ex: Anodynia (anorectal pain) most frequently occurs together with other pain syndromes, like vulvodynia or phallodynia, but sometimes it may be isolated.

ety: Borrowed from Zulu vuvuzela (“to make a vu vu noise”), from the /vuː/ sound the horns make.

s.def: A trumpet-shaped horn, now usually plastic, that produces a loud buzzing sound.
ex: When the Manchester United squad walked through the arrival gates at Durban International yesterday, most players heard a vuvuzela for the first time.
For some, the vuvuzelas herald the country’s piercing emergence from the forced racial hush of apartheid.

s.def: present participle and gerund of vie
present participle and gerund of vy
The act of one who vies; rivalry.
